sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Deadbug Progression is a core stability exercise performed lying on your back with arms and legs in the air.

It involves alternating opposite arm and leg extensions while maintaining a braced core and a flat lower back against the floor.

Widely used in physiotherapy, athletic training, and general fitness, the Deadbug is one of the most effective anti-extension core exercises for building a strong, stable midsection.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Develops deep core stability and anti-extension strength
- Teaches proper bracing and coordination between the upper and lower body
- Low impact and spine-friendly — suitable for all fitness levels
- Improves posture and pelvic control
- Helps prevent lower back pain by strengthening the stabilising muscles
- Enhances motor control and contralateral (opposite side) coordination
- Easily scalable — progressions available for beginners through advanced athletes

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Rectus Abdominis, Transverse Abdominis, Obliques

Secondary: Hip Flexors, Erector Spinae (isometric), Diaphragm, Quadriceps (eccentric control during leg extension)

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Lie flat on your back on an exercise mat or firm surface.
2. Extend both arms straight up toward the ceiling, directly above your shoulders.
3. Lift your legs so your hips and knees are both bent at 90-degree angles, with your shins parallel to the floor.
4. Press your lower back firmly into the floor — there should be no gap between your back and the ground.
5. Engage your core by pulling your belly button in toward your spine.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Take a deep breath and brace your core.
2. Slowly lower your right arm overhead and your left leg toward the floor simultaneously, keeping them just above the ground.
3. Keep your lower back pressed firmly into the floor throughout the entire movement.
4. Pause briefly at the bottom, then return your arm and leg to the starting position.
5. Repeat on the opposite side — lower your left arm and right leg.
6. Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Allowing the lower back to arch off the floor as the limbs extend
- Moving too quickly and losing core control
- Holding the breath instead of maintaining steady breathing
- Extending the limbs too far before building adequate core strength
- Not fully returning to the starting position between reps
- Lifting the head or straining the neck
- Using momentum rather than slow, controlled movement

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Exercise mat or padded surface for comfort
- Clear floor space
- No additional equipment required — this is a bodyweight exercise
- Optional: Small towel or yoga block under the lower back for proprioceptive feedback
- Optional: Resistance band around feet for advanced progression

sections.heading: Progression Levels
sections.content:
1. Beginner: Extend only the legs while keeping both arms stationary overhead.
2. Intermediate: Alternate opposite arm and leg extensions (standard Deadbug).
3. Advanced: Add a slow tempo (3–5 seconds per rep) for increased time under tension.
4. Advanced: Hold a light dumbbell or medicine ball in your hands.
5. Advanced: Wear ankle weights to increase the demand on the core.
6. Always master the current level before progressing — form is paramount.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Back: Firmly pressed into the floor with no arch at any point.
2. Arms: Extended straight up above the shoulders to start.
3. Legs: Hips and knees at 90 degrees, shins parallel to the floor.
4. Core: Braced throughout — imagine pulling your belly button to the floor.
5. Breathing: Exhale as you extend the limbs, inhale as you return.
6. Head: Resting on the floor in a neutral position — do not lift or strain the neck.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Plank: Isometric core hold targeting similar stabilising muscles
- Bird Dog: Opposite arm and leg extension from a hands-and-knees position
- Hollow Body Hold: Anti-extension hold with arms and legs extended
- Pallof Press: Anti-rotation core exercise using cables or bands
- Ab Wheel Rollout: Advanced anti-extension core movement
- Reverse Crunch: Targets lower abdominals with spinal flexion

sections.heading: Deadbug Variations
sections.content:
Standard Deadbug: Alternating opposite arm and leg extensions
Legs-Only Deadbug: Arms stay stationary, only legs extend — beginner variation
Banded Deadbug: Resistance band around feet for added core demand
Weighted Deadbug: Hold a dumbbell or medicine ball for extra resistance
Tempo Deadbug: Slow 3–5 second extensions for increased time under tension
Single-Side Deadbug: Extend same-side arm and leg for a different stability challenge

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lower Back Pain: Ensure your back stays flat — regress to legs-only if needed
Hip Flexor Tightness: Reduce the range of leg extension until mobility improves
Shoulder Mobility Issues: Keep arms bent or reduce overhead range of motion
Neck Strain: Keep your head resting on the floor and avoid lifting
Beginner: Start with legs-only Deadbugs and progress to full alternating once form is solid
Post-Injury: Consult a physiotherapist — the Deadbug is commonly used in rehabilitation programmes
